claim: Class I Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are master regulators of cellular functions.
source: Class I Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are master regulators of cellular functions, with the class IB PI3K catalytic subunit (p110γ) playing key roles in immune signalling.
evidence: This is a general statement about PI3K function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The class IB PI3K catalytic subunit (p110γ) plays key roles in immune signalling.
source: Class I Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are master regulators of cellular functions, with the class IB PI3K catalytic subunit (p110γ) playing key roles in immune signalling.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about p110γ function.

claim: p110γ is a key factor in inflammatory diseases.
source: p110γ is a key factor in inflammatory diseases and has been identified as a therapeutic target for cancers due to its immunomodulatory role.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript discussing p110γ's role in inflammation.

claim: p110γ has been identified as a therapeutic target for cancers due to its immunomodulatory role.
source: p110γ is a key factor in inflammatory diseases and has been identified as a therapeutic target for cancers due to its immunomodulatory role.
evidence: This is supported by references to cancer immunotherapy studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Immunodeficiency and oncogenic mutations of R1021 in the C-terminus can inactivate or activate enzyme activity.
source: Using a combined biochemical/biophysical approach, we have revealed insight into regulation of kinase activity, specifically defining how immunodeficiency and oncogenic mutations of R1021 in the C-terminus can inactivate or activate enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including kinase assays and HDX-MS experiments.

claim: Activation loop-binding inhibitors induce allosteric conformational changes that mimic those in the R1021C mutant.
source: Screening of inhibitors using HDX-MS revealed that activation loop-binding inhibitors induce allosteric conformational changes that mimic those in the R1021C mutant.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing inhibitor-bound wild-type protein to the R1021C mutant.

claim: PI3Ks are lipid kinases that generate the lipid second messenger phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3).
source: PI3Ks are lipid kinases that generate the lipid second messenger phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), which is utilised downstream of cell surface receptors to regulate growth, metabolism, survival, and differentiation (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the citation to Bilanges et al., 2019.

claim: PIP3 is utilised downstream of cell surface receptors to regulate growth, metabolism, survival, and differentiation.
source: PI3Ks are lipid kinases that generate the lipid second messenger phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), which is utilised downstream of cell surface receptors to regulate growth, metabolism, survival, and differentiation (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Bilanges et al., 2019.

claim: PIP3 is generated by four distinct class I PI3K catalytic isoforms separated into two groups: class IA (p110α, p110β, and p110δ) and class IB (p110γ).
source: PIP3, is generated by four distinct class I PI3K catalytic isoforms separated into two groups: class IA (p110α, p110β, and p110δ) and class IB (p110γ).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PI3K classification.

claim: All class I PI3Ks are constitutively associated with regulatory subunits.
source: All class I PI3Ks are constitutively associated with regulatory subunits, and the primary difference between class IA and class IB PI3Ks is their association with unique regulatory subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PI3K structure and regulation.

claim: Class IA PI3Ks bind p85-like regulatory subunits encoded by PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3.
source: Class IA PI3Ks bind p85-like regulatory subunits encoded by PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, and class IB PI3K bind either a p101 or a p84 (also called p87PIKAP) regulatory subunit (Suire et al., 2005; Stephens et al., 1997; Bohnacker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citations provided.

claim: Class IB PI3K bind either a p101 or a p84 (also called p87PIKAP) regulatory subunit.
source: Class IA PI3Ks bind p85-like regulatory subunits encoded by PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, and class IB PI3K bind either a p101 or a p84 (also called p87PIKAP) regulatory subunit (Suire et al., 2005; Stephens et al., 1997; Bohnacker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Suire et al., 2005; Stephens et al., 1997; Bohnacker et al., 2009.

claim: p110α and p110β are ubiquitously expressed.
source: The four catalytic subunits of class I PI3K isoforms have distinct expression profiles: p110α and p110β are ubiquitously expressed, and p110δ and p110γ are mainly localised in immune cells (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Bilanges et al., 2019.

claim: p110δ and p110γ are mainly localised in immune cells.
source: The four catalytic subunits of class I PI3K isoforms have distinct expression profiles: p110α and p110β are ubiquitously expressed, and p110δ and p110γ are mainly localised in immune cells (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Bilanges et al., 2019.

claim: All PI3K isoforms have been implicated in a variety of human diseases, including cancer, immunodeficiencies, inflammation, and developmental disorders.
source: All PI3K isoforms have been implicated in a variety of human diseases, including cancer, immunodeficiencies, inflammation, and developmental disorders (Goncalves et al., 2018; Fruman et al., 2017; Burke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Goncalves et al., 2018; Fruman et al., 2017; Burke, 2018.

claim: The class IB p110γ isoform encoded by PIK3CG is a master regulator of immune cell function.
source: The class IB p110γ isoform encoded by PIK3CG is a master regulator of immune cell function.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the subsequent discussion of p110γ's roles in immune cells.

claim: p110γ carries out almost all its physiological functions in the cell when bound to regulatory subunits.
source: It carries out almost all its physiological functions in the cell when bound to regulatory subunits, with these complexes frequently referred to as PI3Kγ (which can be either p110γ/p101 or p110γ/p84).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about PI3Kγ function.

claim: PI3Kγ plays important roles in the regulation of myeloid (macrophages, mast cells, neutrophils) and lymphoid (T cells, B cells, and Natural Killer cells) -derived immune cells.
source: PI3Kγ plays important roles in the regulation of myeloid (macrophages, mast cells, neutrophils) and lymphoid (T cells, B cells, and Natural Killer cells) -derived immune cells (Camps et al., 2005; Patrucco et al., 2004; Hirsch et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Camps et al., 2005; Patrucco et al., 2004; Hirsch et al., 2000.

claim: PI3Kγ regulates immune cell chemotaxis.
source: It regulates immune cell chemotaxis (Hirsch et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Sasaki et al., 2000a), cytokine release (Laffargue et al., 2002; Collmann et al., 2013), and generation of reactive oxygen species (Hirsch et al., 2000), which are important processes in both the innate and adaptive immune systems.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Hirsch et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Sasaki et al., 2000a.

claim: PI3Kγ regulates cytokine release.
source: It regulates immune cell chemotaxis (Hirsch et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Sasaki et al., 2000a), cytokine release (Laffargue et al., 2002; Collmann et al., 2013), and generation of reactive oxygen species (Hirsch et al., 2000), which are important processes in both the innate and adaptive immune systems.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Laffargue et al., 2002; Collmann et al., 2013.

claim: PI3Kγ regulates generation of reactive oxygen species.
source: It regulates immune cell chemotaxis (Hirsch et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Sasaki et al., 2000a), cytokine release (Laffargue et al., 2002; Collmann et al., 2013), and generation of reactive oxygen species (Hirsch et al., 2000), which are important processes in both the innate and adaptive immune systems.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Hirsch et al., 2000.

claim: The ability of PI3Kγ to mediate multiple immune cell functions is controlled by its activation downstream of numerous cell surface receptors, including G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), the IgE/Antigen receptor, receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), and the Toll-like receptors (TLRs).
source: The ability of PI3Kγ to mediate multiple immune cell functions is controlled by its activation downstream of numerous cell surface receptors, including G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Stoyanov et al., 1995), the IgE/Antigen receptor (Laffargue et al., 2002), receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Schmid et al., 2011), and the Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Luo et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Stoyanov et al., 1995; Laffargue et al., 2002; Schmid et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of PI3Kγ downstream of these stimuli are potentiated by their p84 and p101 regulatory subunits.
source: Activation of PI3Kγ downstream of these stimuli are potentiated by their p84 and p101 regulatory subunits (Bohnacker et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2018; Stephens et al., 1997; Vadas et al., 2013; Kurig et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Bohnacker et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2018; Stephens et al., 1997; Vadas et al., 2013; Kurig et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Patrucco et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in arthritis.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Camps et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in Lupus.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Barber et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in asthma.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Collmann et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in metabolic syndrome.
source: In mouse models, loss of PI3Kγ either genetically or pharmacologically is protective in multiple inflammatory diseases including cardiovascular disease (Patrucco et al., 2004), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), Lupus (Barber et al., 2005), asthma (Collmann et al., 2013), pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis (Thomas et al., 2009; Campa et al., 2018), and metabolic syndrome (Breasson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Breasson et al., 2017.

claim: PI3Kγ is a driver of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma progression through immunomodulatory effects.
source: PI3Kγ is also a driver of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma progression through immunomodulatory effects (Kaneda et al., 2016a), and targeting PI3Kγ in the immune system in combination with checkpoint inhibitors has shown promise in experimental cancer therapy (De Henau et al., 2016; Kaneda et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Kaneda et al., 2016a.

claim: Targeting PI3Kγ in the immune system in combination with checkpoint inhibitors has shown promise in experimental cancer therapy.
source: PI3Kγ is also a driver of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma progression through immunomodulatory effects (Kaneda et al., 2016a), and targeting PI3Kγ in the immune system in combination with checkpoint inhibitors has shown promise in experimental cancer therapy (De Henau et al., 2016; Kaneda et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to De Henau et al., 2016; Kaneda et al., 2016b.

claim: The p110γ enzyme is composed of five domains: a putative uncharacterised adaptor binding domain (ABD), a Ras binding domain (RBD), a C2 domain, a helical domain, and a bi-lobal lipid kinase domain.
source: The p110γ enzyme is composed of five domains, a putative uncharacterised adaptor binding domain (ABD), a Ras binding domain (RBD), a C2 domain, a helical domain, and a bi-lobal lipid kinase domain (Walker et al., 1999; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Walker et al., 1999 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PI3Kγ activation is primarily mediated by Gβγ subunits downstream of GPCR signalling, through a direct interaction of Gβγ with the C2-helical linker of p110γ.
source: PI3Kγ activation is primarily mediated by Gβγ subunits downstream of GPCR signalling, through a direct interaction of Gβγ with the C2-helical linker of p110γ (Vadas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Vadas et al., 2013.

claim: Activation of PI3Kγ by Gβγ requires a secondary interaction between Gβγ and regulatory subunits for physiologically relevant activation.
source: Activation of PI3Kγ by Gβγ requires a secondary interaction between Gβγ and regulatory subunits for physiologically relevant activation (Stephens et al., 1997), with the free p110γ subunit having no detectable activation downstream of GPCR activation in cells (Deladeriere et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Stephens et al., 1997 and Deladeriere et al., 2015.

claim: The free p110γ subunit has no detectable activation downstream of GPCR activation in cells.
source: Activation of PI3Kγ by Gβγ requires a secondary interaction between Gβγ and regulatory subunits for physiologically relevant activation (Stephens et al., 1997), with the free p110γ subunit having no detectable activation downstream of GPCR activation in cells (Deladeriere et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Deladeriere et al., 2015.

claim: PI3Kγ activation can be facilitated by Ras GTPases interacting with the RBD of p110γ.
source: In addition, PI3Kγ activation can be facilitated by Ras GTPases interacting with the RBD of p110γ (Pacold et al., 2000), with the same interface also putatively mediating activation by Rab8 (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Pacold et al., 2000.

claim: The same interface that mediates Ras activation also putatively mediates activation by Rab8.
source: In addition, PI3Kγ activation can be facilitated by Ras GTPases interacting with the RBD of p110γ (Pacold et al., 2000), with the same interface also putatively mediating activation by Rab8 (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Luo et al., 2014.

claim: The C-terminal regulatory motif of the kinase domain is composed of the kα7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 helices that surround the activation loop, and keep the enzyme in an inhibited state.
source: Experiments exploring a novel type II-like kinase inhibitor that targets an active conformation of PI3Kγ revealed novel molecular aspects of regulation involving the C-terminal regulatory motif of the kinase domain, which is composed of the kα7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 helices that surround the activation loop, and keep the enzyme in an inhibited state (Gangadhara et al., 2019; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Gangadhara et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The kα10, kα11, and kα12 helices are sometimes referred to as the regulatory arch.
source: The kα10, kα11, and kα12 helices are sometimes referred to as the regulatory arch (Vadas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Vadas et al., 2011.

claim: Inhibition mediated by the C-terminal regulatory motif is conserved through all class I PI3Ks.
source: Inhibition mediated by the C-terminal regulatory motif is conserved through all class I PI3Ks, although for all other isoforms, this inhibited conformation requires interactions with a p85 regulatory subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A+B; Burke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Burke, 2018 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A+B.

claim: For all class I PI3K isoforms other than p110γ, the inhibited conformation requires interactions with a p85 regulatory subunit.
source: Inhibition mediated by the C-terminal regulatory motif is conserved through all class I PI3Ks, although for all other isoforms, this inhibited conformation requires interactions with a p85 regulatory subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A+B; Burke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Burke, 2018 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A+B.

claim: The activation of all class I PI3Ks is proposed to require a conformational change in the regulatory motif leading to a reorientation of the C-terminus to a conformation that is compatible with membrane binding.
source: The activation of all class I PI3Ks is proposed to require a conformational change in the regulatory motif leading to a reorientation of the C-terminus to a conformation that is compatible with membrane binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Burke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Burke, 2018 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The p110γ catalytic subunit is unique in that it maintains an inactive conformation in the absence of regulatory subunits.
source: The p110γ catalytic subunit is unique in that it maintains an inactive conformation in the absence of regulatory subunits.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about p110γ regulation.

claim: The inactive conformation of p110γ is proposed to be maintained by a Tryptophan lock, where W1080 maintains a closed conformation of the membrane binding C-terminal kα12 helix, leading to an inactive conformation of the activation loop.
source: This conformation is proposed to be maintained by a Tryptophan lock, where W1080 maintains a closed conformation of the membrane binding C-terminal kα12 helix, leading to an inactive conformation of the activation loop (Gangadhara et al., 2019; Figure 1B+D).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Gangadhara et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1B+D.

claim: Disruption of PI3K signalling by either activating or inactivating mutations and deletions are involved in multiple human diseases.
source: Disruption of PI3K signalling by either activating or inactivating mutations and deletions are involved in multiple human diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the subsequent discussion of disease-linked mutations.

claim: Overexpression of any activated class I PI3K isoform can lead to oncogenic transformation.
source: Overexpression of any activated class I PI3K isoform can lead to oncogenic transformation (Kang et al., 2006), although p110α is the most frequently mutated in human disease.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Kang et al., 2006.

claim: p110α is the most frequently mutated class I PI3K isoform in human disease.
source: Overexpression of any activated class I PI3K isoform can lead to oncogenic transformation (Kang et al., 2006), although p110α is the most frequently mutated in human disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activating p110α mutations are linked to both cancer and overgrowth disorders.
source: Activating p110α mutations are linked to both cancer (Samuels et al., 2004; Vasan et al., 2019) and overgrowth disorders (Lindhurst et al., 2012), while activating p110δ mutations are linked to primary immuno-deficiencies (Dornan et al., 2017; Lucas et al., 2016; Angulo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Samuels et al., 2004; Vasan et al., 2019; Lindhurst et al., 2012.

claim: Activating p110δ mutations are linked to primary immuno-deficiencies.
source: Activating p110α mutations are linked to both cancer (Samuels et al., 2004; Vasan et al., 2019) and overgrowth disorders (Lindhurst et al., 2012), while activating p110δ mutations are linked to primary immuno-deficiencies (Dornan et al., 2017; Lucas et al., 2016; Angulo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Dornan et al., 2017; Lucas et al., 2016; Angulo et al., 2013.

claim: A high proportion of activating mutations cluster to the C-terminal regulatory motif of the p110 catalytic subunits.
source: A high proportion of these activating mutations cluster to the C-terminal regulatory motif of the p110 catalytic subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of mutations in the C-terminal regulatory motif.

claim: Multiple p110γ mutations have been identified in cancer patients.
source: Multiple p110γ mutations have been identified in cancer patients (Lowery et al., 2019; AACR Project GENIE Consortium, 2017; Tate et al., 2019), although at a lower frequency than p110α mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Lowery et al., 2019; AACR Project GENIE Consortium, 2017; Tate et al., 2019.

claim: p110γ mutations in cancer patients occur at a lower frequency than p110α mutations.
source: Multiple p110γ mutations have been identified in cancer patients (Lowery et al., 2019; AACR Project GENIE Consortium, 2017; Tate et al., 2019), although at a lower frequency than p110α mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the citations provided.

claim: p110γ loss-of-function mutations in the C-terminal regulatory motif (R1021P, N1085S) have been identified in patients with immunodeficiencies.
source: Intriguingly, p110γ loss-of-function mutations in the C-terminal regulatory motif (R1021P, N1085S) have been identified in patients with immunodeficiencies (Takeda et al., 2019; Thian et al., 2020; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Takeda et al., 2019; Thian et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PI3K mediated diseases being caused by both activating and inactivating mutations highlights the critical role of maintaining appropriate PIP3 levels for human health.
source: PI3K mediated diseases being caused by both activating and inactivating mutations highlights the critical role of maintaining appropriate PIP3 levels for human health.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of both activating and inactivating mutations causing disease.

claim: There are toxicity effects associated with compounds that target all PI3K isoforms by mechanism-based adverse side effects.
source: There are, however, toxicity effects associated with compounds that target all PI3K isoforms by mechanism-based adverse side effects (Fruman and Rommel, 2014), driving the development of isoform selective inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Fruman and Rommel, 2014.

claim: Efforts to develop isoform selective inhibitors have led to multiple clinically approved inhibitors of PI3Kα and PI3Kδ.
source: These efforts have led to multiple clinically approved inhibitors of PI3Kα and PI3Kδ (André et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2014; Flinn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to André et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2014; Flinn et al., 2014.

claim: The critical role of PI3Kγ in inflammation and the tumour microenvironment has stimulated development of PI3Kγ specific inhibitors.
source: The critical role of PI3Kγ in inflammation and the tumour microenvironment has stimulated development of PI3Kγ specific inhibitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of PI3Kγ's role in disease and inhibitor development.

claim: Two main strategies for generating p110γ selective ATP-competitive inhibitors have been established: (i) targeting p110γ-specific pockets in and around the ATP-binding site which are not conserved among p110 isoforms, and (ii) targeting selective p110γ conformational changes.
source: Two main strategies for generating p110γ selective ATP-competitive inhibitors have been established: (i) targeting p110γ-specific pockets in and around the ATP-binding site which are not conserved among p110 isoforms (Collier et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2016), and (ii) targeting selective p110γ conformational changes (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Collier et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2016; Gangadhara et al., 2019.

claim: The conformational selective p110γ inhibitors appear to target its putatively activated conformation.
source: Intriguingly, the conformational selective p110γ inhibitors appear to target its putatively activated conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of conformational selective inhibitors.

claim: The R1021C mutant was ~eightfold more active than wild-type both basally and in the presence of Gβγ.
source: These assays revealed that p110γ/p101 R1021C was ~eightfold more active than wild-type both basally and in the presence of Gβγ, and ~two- to threefold more active upon Ras activation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The R1021C mutant was ~two- to threefold more active than wild-type upon Ras activation.
source: These assays revealed that p110γ/p101 R1021C was ~eightfold more active than wild-type both basally and in the presence of Gβγ, and ~two- to threefold more active upon Ras activation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The R1021C mutant showed a ~eightfold increase in lipid kinase activity compared to wild-type when assaying the free p110γ subunit.
source: The R1021C mutant also showed a ~eightfold increase in lipid kinase activity compared to wild-type when assaying the free 110γ subunit (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The R1021C mutation is consistent with destabilising the regulatory motif, potentially disrupting the Tryptophan lock and leading to increased membrane recruitment.
source: This is consistent with the R1021C mutation destabilising the regulatory motif, potentially disrupting the Tryptophan lock and leading to increased membrane recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinase activity data and structural knowledge.

claim: The R1021P complex showed weak but detectable basal lipid kinase activity.
source: The R1021P complex showed weak but detectable basal lipid kinase activity; however, there was almost no activation by lipidated Gβγ compared to wild-type, suggesting this complex would be almost completely inactive in a physiological context (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The R1021P complex showed almost no activation by lipidated Gβγ compared to wild-type.
source: The R1021P complex showed weak but detectable basal lipid kinase activity; however, there was almost no activation by lipidated Gβγ compared to wild-type, suggesting this complex would be almost completely inactive in a physiological context (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The R1021P complex would be almost completely inactive in a physiological context.
source: The R1021P complex showed weak but detectable basal lipid kinase activity; however, there was almost no activation by lipidated Gβγ compared to wild-type, suggesting this complex would be almost completely inactive in a physiological context (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: R1021P p110γ-p101 showed higher basal ATPase activity compared to wild-type p110γ/p101 and R1021C p110γ-p101.
source: Intriguingly, R1021P p110γ-p101 showed higher basal ATPase activity compared to wild-type p110γ/p101 and R1021C p110γ-p101, revealing that it still has catalytic activity, but almost no activity on membrane substrate (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: R1021P p110γ-p101 still has catalytic activity, but almost no activity on membrane substrate.
source: Intriguingly, R1021P p110γ-p101 showed higher basal ATPase activity compared to wild-type p110γ/p101 and R1021C p110γ-p101, revealing that it still has catalytic activity, but almost no activity on membrane substrate (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The minimal structural features required for ATP hydrolysis are maintained in the R1021P mutant, but either membrane binding or PIP2 recognition is severely impaired.
source: This suggests that the minimal structural features required for ATP hydrolysis are maintained in the R1021P mutant, but that either membrane binding or PIP2 recognition is severely impaired.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATPase and lipid kinase activity data.

claim: The R1021P mutation resulted in large increases in exchange throughout almost the entire C2, helical, and kinase domains.
source: The R1021P mutation resulted in large increases in exchange throughout almost the entire C2, helical, and kinase domains (Figure 2B+D).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2B+D.

claim: For the majority of regions showing increased H/D exchange, the R1021P mutation led to increased exchange at early (3 s) and late timepoints (3000 s) of exchange, indicating that this mutation was leading to significant disruption of protein secondary structure.
source: Comparing the rates of hydrogen exchange between wild-type, R1021C, and R1021P showed many regions where both R1021C and R1021P mutations caused increased H/D exchange. However, for the majority of these regions, the R1021P mutation led to increased exchange at early (3 s) and late timepoints (3000 s) of exchange, indicating that this mutation was leading to significant disruption of protein secondary structure (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The large-scale destabilisation throughout the protein caused by R1021P may explain the low yield and decreased kinase activity.
source: This large-scale destabilisation throughout the protein may explain the low yield and decreased kinase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data and kinase activity data.

claim: The R1021C mutation resulted in increased H/D exchange in the C2, helical and kinase domains of p110γ.
source: The R1021C mutation resulted in increased H/D exchange in the C2, helical and kinase domains of p110γ.
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many of the changes in dynamics of the helical and kinase domains caused by R1021C are similar to those observed upon membrane binding.
source: Intriguingly, many of the changes in dynamics of the helical and kinase domains are similar to those observed upon membrane binding (Vadas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the citation Vadas et al., 2013.

claim: The largest differences in H/D exchange caused by R1021C occurred in the helices in the C-terminal regulatory motif (kα7–12).
source: The largest differences occurred in the helices in the C-terminal regulatory motif (kα7–12) (Figure 2A+C).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2A+C.

claim: A peptide spanning the C-terminal end of the activation loop and kα7 (976–992) showed increased exchange for R1021C, with these changes primarily occurring at later timepoints of exchange (3000 s).
source: A peptide spanning the C-terminal end of the activation loop and kα7 (976–992) showed increased exchange, with these changes primarily occurring at later timepoints of exchange (3000 s) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The increased exchange at later timepoints for R1021C is indicative of these regions maintaining secondary structure, although with increased flexibility.
source: This is indicative of these regions maintaining secondary structure, although with increased flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: The increases in exchange for the R1021C mutant were conserved for the free p110γ subunit, although with larger increases in exchange compared to the p110γ/p101 complex.
source: These increases in exchange for the R1021C mutant were conserved for the free p110γ subunit, although with larger increases in exchange compared to the p110γ/p101 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Larger decreases in exchange with the p101 subunit for the R1021C p110γ compared to WT p110γ suggests a global stabilisation by the p101 subunit that mitigates some of the effects of the R1021C mutant.
source: Intriguingly, we found larger decreases in exchange with the p101 subunit for the R1021C p110γ compared to WT p110γ, which suggests a global stabilisation by the p101 subunit that mitigates some of the effects of the R1021C mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E+F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E+F.

claim: Differences in HDX-MS with R1021C is consistent with a disruption of the inhibitory conformation of the regulatory motif.
source: Differences in HDX-MS with R1021C is consistent with a disruption of the inhibitory conformation of the regulatory motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: The increased dynamics of the activation loop seen in the R1021C mutant may pre-organise the catalytic machinery for activation.
source: In addition, the increased dynamics of the activation loop seen in the mutant may pre-organise the catalytic machinery for activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: Previous HDX-MS analysis of the regulatory mechanisms of class IA PI3Ks revealed that increased dynamics of the activation loop occurred concurrently with increased lipid kinase activity.
source: This is consistent with previous HDX-MS analysis of the regulatory mechanisms of class IA PI3Ks which revealed that increased dynamics of the activation loop occurred concurrently with increased lipid kinase activity (Dornan et al., 2017; Dornan and Burke, 2018; Burke and Williams, 2013; Burke et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Dornan et al., 2017; Dornan and Burke, 2018; Burke and Williams, 2013; Burke et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2011.

claim: Both R1021C and R1021P mutations caused increased exchange in the p101 subunit.
source: The two mutations in R1021C and R1021P both caused increased exchange in the p101 subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Peptides spanning 602–623, and 865–877 of p101 showed similar increases in exchange for both R1021C and R1021P.
source: Peptides spanning 602–623, and 865–877 of p101 showed similar increases in exchange for both R1021C and R1021P, with R1021P also leading to increased exchange in a peptide nearer the N-terminus (102-122) (Figure 2E+F, S3D).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2E+F.

claim: R1021P also led to increased exchange in a peptide nearer the N-terminus (102-122) of p101.
source: Peptides spanning 602–623, and 865–877 of p101 showed similar increases in exchange for both R1021C and R1021P, with R1021P also leading to increased exchange in a peptide nearer the N-terminus (102-122) (Figure 2E+F, S3D).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2E+F.

claim: The increased H/D exchange in p101 may represent increased H/D exchange due to partial destabilisation of the complex.
source: As there is no structural model for the p101 subunit, it is hard to unambiguously interpret this data; however, these may represent increased H/D exchange due to partial destabilisation of the complex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: GaMD simulations revealed increased fluctuations in the residues forming the loop between kα10 and kα11 in the mutated systems, specifically residues T1056, V1057, and G1058 at the C-terminus of kα10.
source: To quantify the effect of mutations on the structural dynamics of p110γ, we calculated the root-mean-square-fluctuation (RMSF) of residues neighbouring the mutation site. RMSF was calculated to determine average flexibility of each residue's Cα and Cβ atoms around their mean position (Figure 3C). This revealed increased fluctuations in the residues forming the loop between kα10 and kα11 in the mutated systems, specifically residues T1056, V1057, and G1058 at the C-terminus of kα10.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutation of R1021 results in disruption of the hydrogen bonding network between R1021 and L1055, T1056, and K1059 in the kα10-kα11 region.
source: Analysis of the simulations revealed that mutation of R1021 results in disruption of the hydrogen bonding network between R1021 and L1055, T1056, and K1059 in the kα10-kα11 region.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data.

claim: Hydrogen bonding occupancies between Y1017 and T1056 decreased from 71% in WT to 56% and 45% in the R1021C and R1021P systems, respectively.
source: Hydrogen bonding occupancies between Y1017 and T1056 decreased from 71% in WT to 56% and 45% in the R1021C and R1021P systems, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data.

claim: Both R1021C and R1021P mutations showed a disruption between C/P1021 and T1024 in the kα8-kα9 backbone hydrogen bonding.
source: Examining the kα8-kα9 backbone hydrogen bonding at the site of mutation, both mutations showed a disruption between C/P1021 and T1024.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data.

claim: The proline mutation showed complete disruption of backbone hydrogen bonds at A1016-L1020 and Y1017-P1021.
source: Additionally, the proline mutation showed complete disruption of backbone hydrogen bonds at A1016-L1020 and Y1017-P1021, decreased bonding occupancy at K1015-A1019 and N1025-I1029, and increased bonding occupancy of Y1017-L1020 and P1021-T1024.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data.

claim: The notable increase in hydrogen bonding disruption in the R1021P compared to R1021C could be responsible for the increased destabilisation observed by HDX-MS.
source: The notable increase in hydrogen bonding disruption in the R1021P compared to R1021C could be responsible for the increased destabilisation observed by HDX-MS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data and HDX-MS data.

claim: The simulations revealed increased angle fluctuations in the mutant simulations between kα8 and kα9, and kα9 and kα10, with a bimodal distribution in the kα8/kα9 angle compared to WT.
source: To obtain further insights into the dynamic behaviour of the C-terminus of the kinase domain and how mutation of R1021 alters conformational dynamics, we monitored the fluctuations of four different angles formed between kα8, kα9, kα10, and kα11 (Figure 3E). The simulations revealed increased angle fluctuations in the mutant simulations between kα8 and kα9, and kα9 and kα10, with a bimodal distribution in the kα8/kα9 angle compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was increased fluctuations in the activation loop in the mutants compared to WT.
source: There was also increased fluctuations in the activation loop in the mutants compared to WT (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MD, HDX-MS, and kinase assays are consistent with the R1021C mutation altering the dynamics of the regulatory motif, and destabilizing the region around the tryptophan lock.
source: Overall, the MD, HDX-MS, and kinase assays are consistent with the R1021C mutation altering the dynamics of the regulatory motif, and destabilizing the region around the tryptophan lock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined MD, HDX-MS, and kinase assay data.

claim: The R1021C mutation may pre-organise the regulatory motif for membrane binding/catalysis.
source: This region must open to allow for membrane binding (Vadas et al., 2013), suggesting that this mutation may pre-organise the regulatory motif for membrane binding/catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data and the citation to Vadas et al., 2013.

claim: The increased H/D exchange in the regulatory motif for the R1021C mutant is similar to previously observed differences caused by cyclopropyl ethyl containing isoindolinone inhibitors.
source: The increased H/D exchange in the regulatory motif for the R1021C mutant is similar to previously observed differences caused by cyclopropyl ethyl containing isoindolinone inhibitors (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the citation Gangadhara et al., 2019.

claim: IPI-549, PIK90, and AS-604850 caused decreased exchange near the active site, with the primary protected region being the hinge region between the N- and C- lobes of the kinase domain.
source: The first group contains the isoquinolinone compound IPI-549, the imidazo[1,2 c]quinazoline molecule PIK-90 and the thiazolidinedione compound AS-604850 (Figure 4A+B). These compounds caused decreased exchange near the active site, with the primary protected region being the hinge region between the N- and C- lobes of the kinase domain (Figure 4B+E).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A+B and Figure 4E.

claim: IPI-549, AS-604850, and PIK-90 showed no (IPI-549, AS-604850) or very small (PIK-90) increases in deuterium incorporation, suggesting that there are localised allosteric conformational changes for these compounds.
source: No (IPI-549, AS-604850) or very small (PIK-90) increases in deuterium incorporation were observed (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), suggesting that there are localised allosteric conformational changes for these compounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Gedatolisib, Omipalisib, and NVS-PI3-4 showed decreased exchange at the active site, but also significant increases in exchange in the kinase and helical domains.
source: The H/D exchange experiments revealed a second class of inhibitors that showed decreased exchange at the active site, but also significant increases in exchange in the kinase and helical domains (Figure 4A+C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F). The second group includes the bis-morpholinotriazine molecule Gedatolisib, difluoro-benzene sulfonamide compound Omipalisib, and the PI3Kγ-specific thiazole derivative NVS-PI3-4.
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A+C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Binding of Gedatolisib, Omipalisib, and NVS-PI3-4 caused increased exchange in multiple regions of the kinase regulatory motif, including kα7, kα10, kα11, and kα12.
source: Binding of these inhibitors caused increased exchange in multiple regions of the kinase regulatory motif, including kα7, kα10, kα11, and kα12.
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data.

claim: For Gedatolisib, the regions of the protein that showed differences in H/D exchange matched very closely to those observed in the R1021C mutant.
source: Intriguingly, for Gedatolisib, the regions of the protein that showed differences in H/D exchange matched very closely to those observed in the R1021C mutant.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the HDX-MS data for Gedatolisib and R1021C.

claim: The conformational changes induced by Gedatolisib, Omipalisib, and NVS-PI3-4 may partially mimic the activated state that occurs in the R1021C mutant.
source: This suggests that the conformational changes induced by these compounds may partially mimic the activated state that occurs in the R1021C mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: AZ2 caused large-scale increased exposure throughout large regions of the helical and kinase domains.
source: Finally, AZ2 caused large-scale increased exposure throughout large regions of the helical and kinase domains (Figure 4A+D), consistent with previous reports (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A+D and the citation to Gangadhara et al., 2019.

claim: AZ2 leads to a complete disruption of secondary structure, with Gedatolisib likely causing increased secondary structure dynamics.
source: Importantly, increased exchange was observed at earlier timepoints for AZ2 compared to Gedatolisib (example peptide 976–992 covering the activation loop and kα7), suggesting that AZ2 leads to a complete disruption of secondary structure, with Gedatolisib likely causing increased secondary structure dynamics (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Multiple PI3K inhibitors can cause large scale allosteric conformational changes upon inhibitor binding.
source: This shows that multiple PI3K inhibitors can cause large scale allosteric conformational changes upon inhibitor binding, however, deciphering the molecular mechanism of these changes were hindered by lack of high-resolution structural information for many of these compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: The crystal structure of p110γ bound to IPI-549 was solved at a resolution of 2.55 Å.
source: To further define the molecular basis for how different inhibitors lead to allosteric conformational changes, we solved the crystal structure of p110γ bound to IPI-549, Gedatolisib, and NVS-PI3-4 at resolutions of 2.55 Å, 2.65 Å, and 3.15 Å, respectively (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: The crystal structure of p110γ bound to Gedatolisib was solved at a resolution of 2.65 Å.
source: To further define the molecular basis for how different inhibitors lead to allosteric conformational changes, we solved the crystal structure of p110γ bound to IPI-549, Gedatolisib, and NVS-PI3-4 at resolutions of 2.55 Å, 2.65 Å, and 3.15 Å, respectively (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: The crystal structure of p110γ bound to NVS-PI3-4 was solved at a resolution of 3.15 Å.
source: To further define the molecular basis for how different inhibitors lead to allosteric conformational changes, we solved the crystal structure of p110γ bound to IPI-549, Gedatolisib, and NVS-PI3-4 at resolutions of 2.55 Å, 2.65 Å, and 3.15 Å, respectively (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: All inhibitors formed the critical hydrogen bond with the amide hydrogen of V882 in the hinge region.
source: All inhibitors formed the critical hydrogen bond with the amide hydrogen of V882 in the hinge region, which is a conserved feature of ATP competitive PI3K kinase inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data.

claim: NVS-PI3-4 leads to opening of a p110γ unique pocket mediated by a conformational change in K883.
source: NVS-PI3-4 leads to opening of a p110γ unique pocket mediated by a conformational change in K883 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G+H).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G+H.

claim: The opening of K883 in p110γ would not be possible in p110α and p110δ as the corresponding K883 residue would clash with the corresponding T955 residue.
source: The opening of K883 is accommodated by it rotating into contact with D884 and T955. This opening would not be possible in p110α and p110δ as the corresponding K883 residue (L829 in p110δ and R852 in p110α) would clash with the corresponding T955 residue (R902 in p110δ and K924 in p110α) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I+J).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I+J.

claim: IPI-549 leads to a conformational change in the orientation of M804, which opens the specificity pocket, primarily composed of W812 and M804.
source: IPI-549 leads to a conformational change in the orientation of M804, which opens the specificity pocket, primarily composed of W812 and M804 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Structure activity analysis of IPI-549 and its derivatives showed a critical role for substitutions at the alkyne position in achieving p110γ specificity.
source: Structure activity analysis of IPI-549 and its derivatives showed a critical role for substitutions at the alkyne position in achieving p110γ specificity (Evans et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Evans et al., 2016.

claim: One of the most striking differences between the structure of Gedatolisib and IPI-549 bound to p110γ is the conformation of the N-terminus of the activation loop, including the residues that make up the DFG motif.
source: One of the most striking differences between the structure of Gedatolisib and IPI-549 bound to p110γ is the conformation of the N-terminus of the activation loop, including the residues that make up the DFG motif (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–F.

claim: Gedatolisib makes extensive contacts with the activation loop, with H967 immediately following the DFG motif in a completely altered conformation.
source: Gedatolisib makes extensive contacts with the activation loop, with H967 immediately following the DFG motif in a completely altered conformation.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data.

claim: The interaction of the cyclopropyl motif in AZ2 with the activation loop has previously been proposed to be critical in mediating allosteric conformational changes.
source: The interaction of the cyclopropyl motif in AZ2 with the activation loop has previously been proposed to be critical in mediating allosteric conformational changes.
evidence: This is supported by previous work on AZ2.

claim: The Gedatolisib structure revealed a disruption of the hydrogen bond between W1080 and D904, with this bond maintained in the IPI-549 structure.
source: In addition to the change in the activation loop, there was a minor perturbation of the W1080 lock, with the Gedatolisib structure revealing a disruption of the hydrogen bond between W1080 and D904, with this bond maintained in the IPI-549 structure (Figure 5F+G).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallography data shown in Figure 5F+G.

claim: The conformational changes induced in the N-terminus of the activation loop may mediate changes in the C-terminus of the activation loop and kα7.
source: The C-terminus of the activation loop and kα7 immediately following showed some of the largest changes upon inhibitor binding in HDX experiments. The kα7 helix is directly in contact with W1080, and we postulated that the conformational changes induced in the N-terminus of the activation loop may mediate these changes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the crystallography and HDX-MS data.

claim: Gedatolisib was roughly threefold more potent for the R1021C mutant over the wild-type.
source: Gedatolisib was roughly threefold more potent for the R1021C mutant over the wild-type, with no significant difference in IC50 values for IPI-549 compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by the IC50 measurement data.

claim: There was no significant difference in IC50 values for IPI-549 between R1021C and wild-type.
source: Gedatolisib was roughly threefold more potent for the R1021C mutant over the wild-type, with no significant difference in IC50 values for IPI-549 compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by the IC50 measurement data.

claim: Understanding the dynamics of activating mutations and inhibitors may be useful as a novel strategy towards designing mutant specific inhibitors.
source: This provides initial insights into how understanding the dynamics of activating mutations and inhibitors may be useful as a novel strategy towards designing mutant specific inhibitors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the IC50 data.

claim: The R1021 residue in the kα8 helix is conserved across all class I PI3Ks.
source: The R1021 in the kα8 helix is conserved across all class I PI3Ks, with it making a number of hydrogen bonds with residues in kα10 and kα11.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and structural data.

claim: R1021 makes a number of hydrogen bonds with residues in kα10 and kα11.
source: The R1021 in the kα8 helix is conserved across all class I PI3Ks, with it making a number of hydrogen bonds with residues in kα10 and kα11.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: Both R1021P and R1021C would lead to disruption of the hydrogen bonds with kα10 and kα11.
source: Both R1021P and R1021C would lead to disruption of the hydrogen bonds with kα10 and kα11, however R1021P would also lead to disruption of the kα8 helix due to the altered dynamics introduced by the proline residue.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge.

claim: R1021P would also lead to disruption of the kα8 helix due to the altered dynamics introduced by the proline residue.
source: Both R1021P and R1021C would lead to disruption of the hydrogen bonds with kα10 and kα11, however R1021P would also lead to disruption of the kα8 helix due to the altered dynamics introduced by the proline residue.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge.

claim: The R1021P mutation greatly destabilised the protein, with purification yields being >20-fold lower than wild-type.
source: The R1021P mutation greatly destabilised the protein, with purification yields being >20-fold lower than wild-type, consistent with greatly decreased p110γ and p101 levels in patient T cells (Takeda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the purification data and the citation to Takeda et al., 2019.

claim: The R1021P mutation is consistent with greatly decreased p110γ and p101 levels in patient T cells.
source: The R1021P mutation greatly destabilised the protein, with purification yields being >20-fold lower than wild-type, consistent with greatly decreased p110γ and p101 levels in patient T cells (Takeda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Takeda et al., 2019.

claim: The R1021P mutation leads to destabilisation of the p110γ protein, leading to both greatly decreased protein levels, and decreased lipid kinase activity.
source: Overall, this data is consistent with this mutation leading to destabilisation of the p110γ protein, leading to both greatly decreased protein levels, and decreased lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data.

claim: The R1021C mutation had enhanced lipid kinase activity, both basally, and upon Gβγ activation.
source: The R1021C mutation, in contrast, had enhanced lipid kinase activity, both basally, and upon Gβγ activation.
evidence: This is supported by the kinase activity data.

claim: HDX-MS and MD simulations suggest that the R1021C activation is mediated by a conformational disruption of the inhibitory c-terminal regulatory motif of the kinase domain.
source: HDX-MS and MD simulations suggest that this activation is mediated by a conformational disruption of the inhibitory c-terminal regulatory motif of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS and MD simulation data.

claim: Many of the changes in the C-terminal regulatory motif caused by R1021C have been previously observed upon membrane binding and upon binding to conformational selective inhibitors.
source: Many of these changes in the C-terminal regulatory motif have been previously observed upon membrane binding (Vadas et al., 2013), as well as upon binding to conformational selective inhibitors (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Vadas et al., 2013 and Gangadhara et al., 2019.

claim: The conformation of the C-terminal regulatory motif is critical in regulating lipid kinase activity, where minor perturbations (R1021C) can lead to disruption of multiple inhibitory contacts allowing for reorientation of the kα12 membrane binding helix and increased lipid kinase activity.
source: The conformation of the C-terminal regulatory motif is critical in regulating lipid kinase activity, where minor perturbations (R1021C) can lead to disruption of multiple inhibitory contacts allowing for reorientation of the kα12 membrane binding helix and increased lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data.

claim: The R1021C mutation can pre-organise the enzyme for productive catalysis, either through increased membrane binding, or increased PIP2 kinase activity.
source: This suggests that the mutation can pre-organise the enzyme for productive catalysis, either through increased membrane binding, or increased PIP2 kinase activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the combined data.

claim: Mutation of the equivalent R992 in PIK3CA to either Leu or Asn has been found in tumour samples.
source: Reinforcing the importance of the R1021 mutant for class I PI3K regulation is the fact that mutation of the equivalent R992 in PIK3CA to either Leu or Asn has been found in tumour samples (Tate et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Tate et al., 2019.

claim: The orientation of the C-terminal regulatory motif is critical in the regulation of all class I PI3Ks.
source: This work corroborates the important role of the C-terminal regulatory motif in controlling PI3K lipid kinase activity. The orientation of this motif is critical in the regulation of all class I PI3Ks, although this is regulated by different molecular mechanisms in p110α, p110β, p110δ, and p110γ.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the data in the manuscript.

claim: The class IA PI3Ks require p85 regulatory subunits to stabilise the C-terminal regulatory motif.
source: The class IA PI3Ks require p85 regulatory subunits to stabilise the C-terminal regulatory motif, with the nSH2 of p85 interacting with and stabilising kα10 for all class IA PI3Ks (Burke and Williams, 2013; Mandelker et al., 2009), and the cSH2 of p85 stabilising kα7, kα8, kα11, and kα12 for p110β and p110δ (Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Burke and Williams, 2013; Mandelker et al., 2009; Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: The nSH2 of p85 interacts with and stabilises kα10 for all class IA PI3Ks.
source: The class IA PI3Ks require p85 regulatory subunits to stabilise the C-terminal regulatory motif, with the nSH2 of p85 interacting with and stabilising kα10 for all class IA PI3Ks (Burke and Williams, 2013; Mandelker et al., 2009), and the cSH2 of p85 stabilising kα7, kα8, kα11, and kα12 for p110β and p110δ (Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Burke and Williams, 2013; Mandelker et al., 2009.

claim: The cSH2 of p85 stabilises kα7, kα8, kα11, and kα12 for p110β and p110δ.
source: The class IA PI3Ks require p85 regulatory subunits to stabilise the C-terminal regulatory motif, with the nSH2 of p85 interacting with and stabilising kα10 for all class IA PI3Ks (Burke and Williams, 2013; Mandelker et al., 2009), and the cSH2 of p85 stabilising kα7, kα8, kα11, and kα12 for p110β and p110δ (Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: The C-terminal regulatory motif of p110γ can be post-translationally modified by phosphorylation of kα9 (T1024) by protein kinase A decreasing lipid kinase activity.
source: The C-terminal regulatory motif of p110γ can be post-translationally modified by phosphorylation of kα9 (T1024) by protein kinase A decreasing lipid kinase activity (Perino et al., 2011), while protein kinase C phosphorylates an adjacent area in the helical domain (S582) (Walser et al., 2013) increasing lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Perino et al., 2011.

claim: Protein kinase C phosphorylates an adjacent area in the helical domain (S582) increasing lipid kinase activity.
source: The C-terminal regulatory motif of p110γ can be post-translationally modified by phosphorylation of kα9 (T1024) by protein kinase A decreasing lipid kinase activity (Perino et al., 2011), while protein kinase C phosphorylates an adjacent area in the helical domain (S582) (Walser et al., 2013) increasing lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Walser et al., 2013.

claim: Fragment screens have revealed potential druggable pockets that may be targeted in class IA PI3Ks.
source: Although no allosteric inhibitors that bind out of the ATP-binding pocket have been developed, fragment screens have revealed potential druggable pockets that may be targeted in class IA PI3Ks (Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Miller et al., 2017.

claim: PI3Kγ can be selectively targeted through a conformationally selective inhibitor, AZ2.
source: It has previously been noted that PI3Kγ can be selectively targeted through a conformationally selective inhibitor, AZ2 (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Gangadhara et al., 2019.

claim: This work provides novel insights into how the C-terminal regulatory motif of PI3Kγ regulates lipid kinase activity.
source: Overall, this work provides novel insights into how the C-terminal regulatory motif of PI3Kγ regulates lipid kinase activity, how oncogenic and immunodeficiency mutations can disrupt this regulation, and how one can exploit these conformational changes to develop isoform and mutant selective small molecule inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the work's contributions.

claim: This work provides novel insights into how oncogenic and immunodeficiency mutations can disrupt regulation of PI3Kγ lipid kinase activity.
source: Overall, this work provides novel insights into how the C-terminal regulatory motif of PI3Kγ regulates lipid kinase activity, how oncogenic and immunodeficiency mutations can disrupt this regulation, and how one can exploit these conformational changes to develop isoform and mutant selective small molecule inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the work's contributions.

claim: This work provides novel insights into how one can exploit conformational changes to develop isoform and mutant selective small molecule inhibitors.
source: Overall, this work provides novel insights into how the C-terminal regulatory motif of PI3Kγ regulates lipid kinase activity, how oncogenic and immunodeficiency mutations can disrupt this regulation, and how one can exploit these conformational changes to develop isoform and mutant selective small molecule inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the work's contributions.
